nature-found-096.title: How much humanity takes from the biosphere
nature-found-096.text:
{{ref:nature-hist-028}} reduces the whole question of lasting prosperity to a comparison. On one side is what humanity asks of the biosphere: its products and services, plus its use as a dump. On the other is the rate at which the biosphere regenerates. When the ask exceeds regeneration, the biosphere depreciates.

The framing builds on Ehrlich and Holdren's 1971 split of impact into the number of people, individual wants and the technologies and institutions in play. Their impact, humanity's draw per unit of time, is today known as the {{ref:nature-acct-027}}. It takes two forms: harvesting for use and production, and using the biosphere as a sink for {{ref:nature-eecon-231}}.

Both extraction X and waste Z grow with people times {{ref:nature-econ-491}} per capita, divided by efficiency terms: X = Ny/alpha_X and Z = Ny/alpha_Z. Earnings stand in for human activity, though they almost surely understate it. Over the long run, the total taken must equal what the biosphere can sustainably provide, and uncovering that relation is the heart of the Review.

nature-found-091.title: Produced, human and natural capital: three kinds of wealth
nature-found-091.text:
Roads and patents, skills and a sea view: {{ref:nature-hist-028}} sorts all of them into three kinds of capital goods. The word capital has not always been so generous. Economists confine it to assets that are measurable, and the range has widened over time.

Roads, buildings, machines, ports and patents are tangible or intangible but alienable, meaning they can be sold on. Together they are called produced capital. Health, education and skills are intangible and cannot be handed to someone else. They form human capital, which entered the list once ways were found to measure its value to individuals and society.

Natural capital, introduced earlier as {{ref:nature-found-010}}, became the third category once methods existed to measure the value people place on natural resources. It runs from plants, which are tangible and alienable, to pollinators, a sea view and the global climate, which are intangible and not alienable.

The Review stresses a wedge between the market prices of these goods, especially natural capital, and their accounting prices. An accounting price, or shadow price, is the contribution an extra unit makes to the flow of social benefits. Many kinds of natural capital have no market and are free to the user, so special methods are needed to estimate it. Mainstream growth and development theories, and the models used by finance ministries and central banks, leave out humanity's dependence on Nature.
